title: Reproducible NGS workshop — extracted scripts (Day 0–4)
text:
This package was generated from the five supplied Quarto lessons without changing the scientific workflow. Day 0 is setup; Days 1–3 are core practicals; Day 4 is an optional R integration exercise.


Each dayN/ contains: - source_quarto.qmd: complete original lesson. - scripts/: complete individual Bash/R scripts, with their original workshop-relative paths. - dayN_docker_calls.sh: Docker invocations from that day, in source order, with # Step comments and corresponding Quarto line numbers. - dayN_terminal_examples.md: other terminal examples, inspection commands, and demonstrations.



These are not standalone data bundles. Commands assume the existing workshop_ngs repository, sequencing data, reference files, and results, with the relative paths described in the Quarto lessons. They are designed to run from the repository root, not from within dayN/.

Copy the script directories into the existing project while keeping the nested paths. On Linux/macOS/WSL, from this extracted ZIP directory, for example:
mkdir -p ~/workshop_ngs/scripts
for day in day1 day2 day3 day4; do
  if [ -d "$day/scripts" ]; then cp -R "$day/scripts/." ~/workshop_ngs/scripts/; fi
done
Change directory to the workshop repo: cd ~/workshop_ngs.
Review the original lesson, create required folders and download prerequisite files as described there. The dayN_terminal_examples.md is a reference for the terminal checks and setup commands.
Open the day’s dayN_docker_calls.sh, review optional/alternative Docker routes, then run selected commands from the file in lesson order. Do not execute the entire file without reviewing alternatives, internet tests and interactive examples.

The Day 2 Docker calls additionally include a clearly marked non-interactive Rscript invocation to run the complete extracted DESeq2 analysis.
Day 1 includes alternative ENA and SRA FASTQ acquisition routes; choose the route described for your setup. Day 0 has platform-specific setup. Day 4 is optional.
Important: Script code is extracted from the provided teaching notes, not verified against installed container images or datasets. Some snippets in the notes are intentionally interactive or conceptual, and are retained separately rather than made into misleading runnable scripts. The collected Docker calls are not a dependency-resolving automated workflow.

title: ChIP-seq Concepts
text: ChIP-seq measures enrichment of protein-associated DNA fragments. A matched input samples fragmentation, mappability, copy-number, and library background before immunoprecipitation; a mock or target-negative IP addresses different nonspecific background. title: Reference Genomes
text:
Pairing rule
Use genome and annotation files from the same source and release whenever possible. Mismatched references are a common source of failed counting and broken interval annotation.
The workshop reference bundle is NCBI RefSeq assembly GCF_025998455.1 (ASM2599845v1) for H. pylori strain CHC155. Its chromosome accession is NZ_AP026446.1. The FASTA, GFF3, and GTF files are downloaded together from the same NCBI assembly directory; GFF3 is the primary annotation used by featureCounts and Day 4 interval analysis. Day 1 also converts its intron-free gene rows into the matched 12-column reference_genome/genes.bed file used for RSeQC strandedness inference, records provenance in reference_genome/REFERENCE.md, and records source-file content in reference_genome/reference_files.sha256.
Processed files using another coordinate system are not compatible with this workshop reference. Raw reads must be remapped and all downstream coordinates regenerated.

title: Containers with Docker
text:
Scripts that require specialist bioinformatics tools run inside the Docker image that contains the required tool. The script contains the analysis logic; the Docker command only chooses the software environment and mounts the project folder:
docker run --rm \
  --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$PWD:/work" \
  -w /work \
  docker.io/fgualdr/ngs-fastp@sha256:67d843e80a94d529e9fbcc8e0767c3e018f62c1c9560087214dc1db998b74650 \
  bash scripts/day1/03_trim_fastq.sh
The @sha256:... suffix is an immutable content digest. A tag such as latest can be moved to new content, so a tag alone does not identify the exact environment. The course records its release image set in Docker_files/images.lock.tsv. Dockerfiles remain useful build recipes, but live package repositories can resolve differently during a later rebuild unless their dependencies are also locked.
Day 1 download scripts are the exception: because they require only Bash and standard commands such as curl, awk, and gzip, they run directly on the host. Their lesson sections show the curl image only as an optional fallback and explain the DNS, proxy, or VPN issues that can affect network access from inside Docker.

title: Containers with Docker
text:
Why this matters
The image provides software. The mounted project folder provides persistent files. docker run --rm starts a temporary container, runs the script inside /work, writes outputs into the mounted project folder, and removes the container when the command finishes. This separation makes the analysis portable across macOS, Linux, and Windows WSL2.

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
text:
ImportantThis entire page is optional



Day 4 is an optional extension for students who want to practise basic genomic integration in R. It is not required to complete the core FASTQ-to-result workflows from Days 1–3.

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
text:
1. Aim
The goal is not to build a complete regulatory-network pipeline. The goal is to understand a small set of reusable R/Bioconductor objects and operations:





flowchart TD
    inputs["Import DESeq2 results + consensus peaks + gene annotation"]
    objects["Represent genomic intervals as GRanges"]
    links["Find nearest genes + promoter overlaps"]
    joined["Join peak-gene links with RNA-seq results"]
    fasta["Retrieve peak DNA from indexed FASTA"]
    sequence["DNAStringSet peak sequences"]
    composition["Calculate GC fraction + CpG counts"]

    inputs --> objects
    objects --> links
    links --> joined
    joined --> fasta
    fasta --> sequence
    sequence --> composition






By the end, you should be able to explain:

why a regular table and a genomic interval object are different;
how BED and GFF3 become GRanges objects;
how distanceToNearest() and findOverlaps() answer different questions;
how promoter windows depend on strand;
how an indexed FASTA can supply peak DNA sequences;
how to calculate GC fraction and CpG counts;
why a peak near a differentially expressed gene is a candidate relationship, not proof of direct regulation.

section: 3. The four object types used today
text:
3. The four object types used today








R object
Represents
Typical operation




data.frame
rectangular statistics or metadata
filter, sort, merge


GRanges
genomic intervals plus metadata
overlap, nearest, distance, resize


Hits
index pairs connecting two interval sets
query and subject extraction


FaFile / DNAStringSet
indexed genome on disk / sequences in memory
retrieve bases, count letters and motifs



The distinction matters. A data.frame knows that a column is named start, but it does not know that start, end, chromosome and strand form a genomic interval. GRanges does.

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
text:
6. Nearest gene: a distance question
distanceToNearest() returns a Hits object. Each hit connects one query peak to one nearest subject gene and stores the distance.
Add:
nearest_hits <- distanceToNearest(peaks, genes, ignore.strand = TRUE)
class(nearest_hits)
nearest_hits
Convert the index pairs into a readable table:
nearest_table <- data.frame(
  peak_id = peaks$peak_id[queryHits(nearest_hits)],
  peak_chrom = as.character(seqnames(peaks))[queryHits(nearest_hits)],
  peak_start = start(peaks)[queryHits(nearest_hits)],
  peak_end = end(peaks)[queryHits(nearest_hits)],
  gene_id = genes$gene_id[subjectHits(nearest_hits)],
  gene_strand = as.character(strand(genes))[subjectHits(nearest_hits)],
  distance_to_gene = mcols(nearest_hits)$distance
)

write.table(
  nearest_table,
  file.path(table_dir, "peak_nearest_gene.tsv"),
  sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)
Interpretation:

distance 0 means that the peak overlaps the gene interval;
a positive distance means that the peak is outside the gene body;
“nearest” does not mean “regulated.” It is a geometric annotation rule.

Plot the distance distribution:
distance_plot <- ggplot(nearest_table, aes(distance_to_gene)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Distance from peak to nearest annotated gene (bp)",
    y = "Number of peaks"
  )

ggsave(
  file.path(plot_dir, "peak_to_nearest_gene_distance.pdf"),
  distance_plot,
  width = 7, height = 5
)

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
text:
7. Promoter overlap: an interval-overlap question
For this optional exercise, define a strand-aware promoter as 500 bp upstream and 100 bp downstream of the annotated gene start.
promoters() understands gene strand:
promoter_ranges <- promoters(genes, upstream = 500, downstream = 101)
promoter_ranges <- trim(promoter_ranges)
promoter_ranges$gene_id <- genes$gene_id
For a +-strand gene, the promoter extends toward smaller coordinates. For a --strand gene, upstream extends toward larger coordinates.
Find peak-promoter overlaps:
promoter_hits <- findOverlaps(peaks, promoter_ranges, ignore.strand = TRUE)
class(promoter_hits)
Build a table:
promoter_table <- data.frame(
  peak_id = peaks$peak_id[queryHits(promoter_hits)],
  peak_chrom = as.character(seqnames(peaks))[queryHits(promoter_hits)],
  peak_start = start(peaks)[queryHits(promoter_hits)],
  peak_end = end(peaks)[queryHits(promoter_hits)],
  gene_id = promoter_ranges$gene_id[subjectHits(promoter_hits)],
  promoter_start = start(promoter_ranges)[subjectHits(promoter_hits)],
  promoter_end = end(promoter_ranges)[subjectHits(promoter_hits)],
  gene_strand = as.character(strand(promoter_ranges))[subjectHits(promoter_hits)]
)

write.table(
  promoter_table,
  file.path(table_dir, "peak_promoter_overlaps.tsv"),
  sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)
One peak can overlap more than one promoter, especially in a compact bacterial genome with divergent or closely spaced genes. That is a biological ambiguity, not a software error.

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
section: 8. Join promoter-associated peaks to RNA-seq results
text:
8. Join promoter-associated peaks to RNA-seq results
The interval operation produced a regular table. We can now merge it with the DESeq2 result table by gene identifier.
First confirm the RNA-seq identifier column:
if (!"gene_id" %in% names(rna)) {
  names(rna)[1] <- "gene_id"
}
rna$gene_id <- as.character(rna$gene_id)
Join and classify candidate relationships:
integrated <- merge(promoter_table, rna, by = "gene_id", all.x = TRUE)

integrated$is_de <- !is.na(integrated$padj) &
  integrated$padj < 0.05 &
  abs(integrated$log2FoldChange) >= 1

integrated$candidate_class <- ifelse(
  integrated$is_de,
  "DE gene with promoter-overlapping peak",
  "promoter-overlapping peak without DE evidence"
)

write.table(
  integrated,
  file.path(table_dir, "promoter_peak_rnaseq_integration.tsv"),
  sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)

candidate_targets <- integrated[integrated$is_de, , drop = FALSE]
candidate_targets <- candidate_targets[order(candidate_targets$padj), , drop = FALSE]

write.table(
  candidate_targets,
  file.path(table_dir, "candidate_regulatory_relationships.tsv"),
  sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)
The phrase candidate regulatory relationship is deliberate. Promoter-proximal occupancy plus differential expression is stronger combined evidence than either result alone, but it does not establish causality or distinguish direct from indirect effects without additional evidence.

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
text:
9. Optional: add Day 3 differential-peak statistics
When the Day 3 differential-peak table exists, join ChIP-seq and RNA-seq effect estimates by peak_id and gene_id.
Add:
if (file.exists(peak_de_file)) {
  peak_de <- read.delim(peak_de_file, check.names = FALSE)

  peak_de_small <- peak_de[, c(
    "peak_id", "log2FoldChange", "padj", "significant"
  )]

  names(peak_de_small)[names(peak_de_small) == "log2FoldChange"] <- "chip_log2FoldChange"
  names(peak_de_small)[names(peak_de_small) == "padj"] <- "chip_padj"
  names(peak_de_small)[names(peak_de_small) == "significant"] <- "chip_significant"

  rna_chip <- merge(integrated, peak_de_small, by = "peak_id", all.x = TRUE)
  names(rna_chip)[names(rna_chip) == "log2FoldChange"] <- "rna_log2FoldChange"
  names(rna_chip)[names(rna_chip) == "padj"] <- "rna_padj"

  write.table(
    rna_chip,
    file.path(table_dir, "rna_chip_peak_integration.tsv"),
    sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
  )

  plot_dt <- rna_chip[
    is.finite(rna_chip$rna_log2FoldChange) &
      is.finite(rna_chip$chip_log2FoldChange),
    , drop = FALSE
  ]

  if (nrow(plot_dt) > 0) {
    effect_plot <- ggplot(plot_dt, aes(chip_log2FoldChange, rna_log2FoldChange)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
      geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
      theme_bw() +
      labs(
        x = "ChIP-seq peak log2 fold change",
        y = "RNA-seq gene log2 fold change"
      )

    ggsave(
      file.path(plot_dir, "rna_vs_chip_log2foldchange.pdf"),
      effect_plot,
      width = 6, height = 5
    )
  }
}
The four quadrants are descriptive, not automatically activating/repressing mechanisms. Condition-dependent occupancy and expression can be related through many direct and indirect processes.

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
section: 10. Retrieve peak DNA from the FASTA
text:
10. Retrieve peak DNA from the FASTA
FaFile keeps the genome on disk. scanFa() retrieves only the requested GRanges intervals and returns a DNAStringSet.
Add:
open(genome)
peak_sequences <- scanFa(genome, param = peaks)
close(genome)

names(peak_sequences) <- peaks$peak_id
class(peak_sequences)
peak_sequences[1:3]
The objects now have complementary roles:
peaks          = where the intervals are
peak_sequences = which DNA bases occur in those intervals

title: Optional Day 4 - Basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq integration in R
section: 11. Calculate GC fraction and CpG counts
text:
11. Calculate GC fraction and CpG counts
GC fraction is the proportion of bases that are G or C. CpG count is the number of exact CG dinucleotides.
Add:
base_counts <- letterFrequency(
  peak_sequences,
  letters = c("A", "C", "G", "T"),
  as.prob = FALSE
)

sequence_width <- width(peak_sequences)
gc_fraction <- (base_counts[, "G"] + base_counts[, "C"]) / sequence_width
cpg_count <- vcountPattern("CG", peak_sequences, fixed = TRUE)

sequence_table <- data.frame(
  peak_id = names(peak_sequences),
  width = sequence_width,
  A = base_counts[, "A"],
  C = base_counts[, "C"],
  G = base_counts[, "G"],
  T = base_counts[, "T"],
  GC_fraction = gc_fraction,
  CpG_count = cpg_count,
  CpG_per_100bp = 100 * cpg_count / sequence_width
)

write.table(
  sequence_table,
  file.path(table_dir, "peak_sequence_composition.tsv"),
  sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)
Plot simple distributions:
gc_plot <- ggplot(sequence_table, aes(GC_fraction)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "GC fraction", y = "Number of peaks")

ggsave(
  file.path(plot_dir, "peak_GC_fraction.pdf"),
  gc_plot,
  width = 6, height = 4
)

cpg_plot <- ggplot(sequence_table, aes(CpG_per_100bp)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "CpG dinucleotides per 100 bp", y = "Number of peaks")

ggsave(
  file.path(plot_dir, "peak_CpG_density.pdf"),
  cpg_plot,
  width = 6, height = 4
)
Sequence composition can help diagnose motif and background effects. It does not by itself show protein binding or regulatory function.

title: Day 2 - RNA-seq from FASTQ to differential expression
text:
3. Reference-based RNA-seq FASTQ mapping
RNA-seq mapping asks where each sequenced read, or read pair, fits on a reference sequence. The input is FASTQ. The output is an alignment file that records the genomic position and alignment details for each read.
Mapping starts from:

trimmed FASTQ files from Day 1;
a reference genome FASTA;
an aligner index built from that FASTA.

The index does not change the genome. It creates extra files that allow the aligner to search the genome quickly.

3.1 Alignment versus pseudoalignment
Full aligners try to place each read or read pair at one or more genomic or transcriptomic coordinates. A common strategy is seed-and-extend:

split or sample short exact pieces of the read called seeds;
use the index to find candidate reference positions for those seeds;
extend candidate alignments across the full read;
score each alignment using matches, mismatches, gaps, clipping, base qualities, and sometimes paired-end consistency;
report the best alignment or alignments, usually with a mapping quality score.

The exact scoring system differs by tool. In general, a better score means the read agrees better with the reference. If several locations have similar scores, the read is ambiguous and the mapping quality is lower. For paired-end reads, aligners also use whether both mates map with the expected orientation and distance.
Splice-aware RNA-seq aligners add another idea: a read may align across two exons with a skipped intron between them. These aligners can represent exon-exon junctions in the alignment. This is essential for many eukaryotic RNA-seq datasets but unnecessary for this bacterial workshop.
Pseudoaligners and quasi-aligners usually do not try to report one exact genomic coordinate for every read. Instead, they infer which transcript or set of transcripts is compatible with each read or fragment. This is very fast and useful for transcript quantification, but it is a different workflow from creating genome-coordinate BAM files for IGV and feature counting.
Common genome aligners include:











Tool
Main alignment idea
Splice-aware?
Main strengths
Main limitations
Take home




Bowtie2
FM-index genome aligner using seed-and-extend search and gapped alignment scoring
No
Fast, simple, low memory, good for small genomes; supports mismatches, gaps, clipping, and paired-end constraints; produces coordinate BAM files
Does not model exon-exon junctions as splicing events; eukaryotic exon-internal reads can map, but junction-spanning reads are not handled like a splice-aware RNA-seq aligner
Good default here for bacterial RNA-seq and ChIP-seq because the genome is small and introns are not present


BWA-MEM/BWA-MEM2
Burrows-Wheeler genome aligner optimized for longer reads using maximal exact matches as seeds
No
Very robust general-purpose DNA aligner; common for variant calling, genomic DNA, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and microbial genome alignment
Not designed to discover splice junctions; less commonly used as the main tool for gene-level RNA-seq counting
Conceptually similar to Bowtie2 as a non-splice-aware genome aligner, but more associated with DNA-seq and longer-read genomic alignment


STAR
Splice-aware RNA-seq genome aligner using an uncompressed suffix-array style index and two-pass-style junction discovery options
Yes
Extremely fast for large eukaryotic RNA-seq; strong exon-junction detection; widely used for mammalian gene-count workflows
High memory use; more complex; unnecessary for bacterial genomes without introns
A standard choice for mammalian or other eukaryotic RNA-seq when exon-exon junctions matter


HISAT2
Splice-aware RNA-seq genome aligner using hierarchical FM indexes, with optional transcript/splice-site guidance
Yes
Much lower memory than STAR; good eukaryotic splice-aware alignment; can use known splice sites while still discovering novel junctions
Often slower than STAR for large projects; still more complex than needed for this bacterial workflow
A compact splice-aware alternative for eukaryotic RNA-seq, especially when memory is limited



Common pseudoalignment or quasi-alignment tools include:










Tool
Method used by the tool
Advantages
Disadvantages
When to use it




Salmon
Quasi-mapping or selective alignment to transcript sequences
Very fast transcript/gene quantification
Usually does not create a genome-coordinate BAM for IGV; requires transcriptome and transcript-to-gene handling
Transcript-level quantification


Kallisto
Pseudoalignment to transcript compatibility classes
Very fast and lightweight
Usually does not create a genome-coordinate BAM for IGV; less natural for the BAM-first workflow used here
Fast transcript quantification



In this workshop we use Bowtie2 because H. pylori has a small bacterial genome, there are no introns to model, and we want coordinate-sorted BAM files that can also be inspected later in IGV.


3.2 SAM and BAM files
The general alignment file created by an aligner is SAM:
Sequence Alignment/Map format
SAM is a plain-text alignment format. BAM is the compressed binary version of SAM. In practice, we usually create a temporary SAM file, convert it to BAM, sort the BAM by genomic coordinate, and create a BAM index file:
sample.sam
  -> sample.sorted.bam
  -> sample.sorted.bam.bai
The sorted BAM is compact and fast for downstream tools. The .bai index lets software jump directly to one genomic region without reading the whole BAM file.
A BAM file contains one alignment record per read alignment. The common SAM/BAM fields are:







Field
Meaning




QNAME
Read name from the FASTQ identifier


FLAG
Bit-coded alignment status, such as paired, mapped, reverse strand, secondary, supplementary, duplicate


RNAME
Reference sequence name, such as chromosome or contig


POS
1-based leftmost alignment coordinate


MAPQ
Mapping quality, a score for confidence in the reported position


CIGAR
Compact description of matches, insertions, deletions, clipping, and skipped reference regions


RNEXT
Reference name for the mate read in paired-end data


PNEXT
Position of the mate read


TLEN
Template length inferred from the read pair


SEQ
Read sequence


QUAL
Base quality string



The CIGAR string is important for RNA-seq. In bacterial RNA-seq, reads usually align continuously because bacterial genes usually do not contain spliceosomal introns. In eukaryotic RNA-seq, a read can span an exon-exon junction. Splice-aware aligners represent this with an N operation in the CIGAR string, meaning a skipped region in the reference. Other CIGAR operations include M for aligned match/mismatch, I for insertion relative to the reference, D for deletion relative to the reference, and S for soft clipping.
Aligners also write optional tags after the common columns. These tags are tool-specific. Common examples include edit distance, alignment score, number of possible alignments, or strand information. This is one reason BAM files from different aligners can contain the same core information but different additional descriptors.


3.3 How paired-end reads are stored in BAM
Paired-end FASTQ files have one R1 file and one R2 file. In the BAM file, the two ends are not stored as one combined row. They are stored as two separate alignment records with the same read name (QNAME), one record for read 1 and one record for read 2.
The pair relationship is encoded in the BAM fields:







BAM field
Paired-end meaning




QNAME
Same read-pair identifier for R1 and R2


FLAG
Says whether this record is read 1 or read 2, whether the mate is mapped, whether the pair is properly paired, and which strand each end maps to


RNAME and POS
Reference name and position for this read end


RNEXT and PNEXT
Reference name and position for the mate read


TLEN
Inferred template length, meaning the genomic span covered by the read pair


CIGAR
Alignment shape for this read end only



For a simple properly paired fragment, R1 and R2 usually map to nearby positions on opposite strands with an expected orientation. The two BAM records point to each other through the mate fields. When we sort a BAM by coordinate, the two mates may no longer be next to each other in the file, but the mate information remains encoded in the records.
This is why paired-end tools can count fragments rather than individual read ends. Later, featureCounts uses the paired-end information to assign one fragment-level count to a gene instead of counting R1 and R2 separately.


3.4 Build the Bowtie2 index
Bowtie2 must search for possible locations for millions of reads. Searching the FASTA sequence from beginning to end for every read would be inefficient, so bowtie2-build converts the reference genome into compact index files that Bowtie2 can search quickly. We build the index once for this exact genome and reuse it for every RNA-seq and ChIP-seq sample; if the reference FASTA changes, the index must be rebuilt.
This reference-genome index is different from the .bai index described above: the Bowtie2 index makes the genome searchable before alignment, whereas a .bai file makes an aligned BAM searchable by genomic position afterward.
Create scripts/day2_rnaseq/01_build_bowtie2_index.sh:
nano scripts/day2_rnaseq/01_build_bowtie2_index.sh
Paste this script:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

genome="reference_genome/genome.fa"
index_prefix="reference_genome/bowtie2_index/genome"

mkdir -p reference_genome/bowtie2_index

bowtie2-build \
  --threads 2 \
  "${genome}" \
  "${index_prefix}"
Run it:
docker run --rm \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/work" \
  -w /work \
  docker.io/fgualdr/ngs-bowtie2-samtools \
  bash scripts/day2_rnaseq/01_build_bowtie2_index.sh


3.5 Map RNA-seq reads
The mapping script uses the Day 1 trimmed RNA-seq FASTQ files. It writes Bowtie2 logs, sorted BAM files, BAM indexes, and samtools mapping summaries.
Create scripts/day2_rnaseq/02_map_bowtie2_sort_index.sh:
nano scripts/day2_rnaseq/02_map_bowtie2_sort_index.sh
Paste this script:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

fastq_dir="results/day1_qc/trimmed_fastq/rnaseq"
index_prefix="reference_genome/bowtie2_index/genome"
bam_dir="results/day2_rnaseq/bam"
log_dir="results/logs/day2"

mkdir -p "${bam_dir}" "${log_dir}"

for read1 in "${fastq_dir}"/*_R1.trimmed.fastq.gz
do
  [[ -e "${read1}" ]] || continue

  read2="${read1/_R1.trimmed.fastq.gz/_R2.trimmed.fastq.gz}"
  sample_id="$(basename "${read1}" _R1.trimmed.fastq.gz)"
  sam_file="${bam_dir}/${sample_id}.sam"
  bam_file="${bam_dir}/${sample_id}.sorted.bam"
  filtered_bam="${bam_dir}/${sample_id}.filtered.bam"

  if [[ ! -f "${read2}" ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: paired read not found for ${read1}" >&2
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "Mapping ${sample_id}"
  bowtie2 \
    -x "${index_prefix}" \
    -1 "${read1}" \
    -2 "${read2}" \
    -p 2 \
    -S "${sam_file}" \
    2> "${log_dir}/${sample_id}.bowtie2.log"

  # Convert the SAM alignments to a coordinate-sorted BAM.
  # samtools sort accepts SAM input directly; -O BAM makes the output format explicit.
  samtools sort \
    -@ 2 \
    -O BAM \
    -o "${bam_file}" \
    "${sam_file}"

  samtools index "${bam_file}"

  samtools flagstat "${bam_file}" > "${log_dir}/${sample_id}.flagstat.txt"

  samtools view \
    -@ 2 \
    -b \
    -q 10 \
    -f 2 \
    -F 2828 \
    -o "${filtered_bam}" \
    "${bam_file}"

  samtools index "${filtered_bam}"

  samtools flagstat "${filtered_bam}" > "${log_dir}/${sample_id}.filtered.flagstat.txt"

  rm -f "${sam_file}"
done
The loop performs the following steps for each paired-end sample.
trimmed R1 + R2
  -> Bowtie2 mapping -> temporary SAM + Bowtie2 log
  -> samtools sort -> coordinate-sorted BAM
  -> samtools index + flagstat
  -> samtools view filtering -> filtered BAM
  -> samtools index + flagstat
  -> remove temporary SAM

3.5.1 Map the paired reads
bowtie2 uses the Bowtie2 index (-x) and the trimmed R1/R2 files (-1 and -2) to find genomic alignments. It writes:

a temporary SAM file containing the alignments;
a Bowtie2 log containing the alignment summary.

The log is written separately with 2> because Bowtie2 sends its progress and summary information to the standard-error stream.


3.5.2 Convert SAM to a coordinate-sorted BAM
samtools sort reads the text SAM file directly and writes a coordinate-sorted BAM. The -O BAM option makes the output format explicit:
samtools sort \
  -@ 2 \
  -O BAM \
  -o "${bam_file}" \
  "${sam_file}"
Conversion and sorting therefore happen in the same command. Coordinate sorting places alignments from the same genomic region together, which is required for BAM indexing and makes downstream access efficient.


3.5.3 Index and summarize the sorted BAM
samtools index creates sample.sorted.bam.bai. This index allows programs to jump directly to one genomic region without reading the complete BAM.
samtools flagstat then creates the first mapping summary. It reports totals such as mapped reads and properly paired reads before we apply alignment filters.


3.5.4 Filter alignments for counting
The script creates a second BAM containing the alignments we want to use for gene counting:
samtools view \
  -@ 2 \
  -b \
  -q 10 \
  -f 2 \
  -F 2828 \
  -o "${filtered_bam}" \
  "${bam_file}"







Option
Meaning




-b
Write BAM output


-q 10
Keep alignments with mapping quality of at least 10


-f 2
Require the read to belong to a properly aligned pair


-F 2828
Exclude unmapped reads, reads whose mate is unmapped, secondary alignments, failed-QC reads, and supplementary alignments



SAM flags are bit-coded and do not need to be memorized. The Picard flag converter can be used to inspect a filter.
We do not exclude reads marked as duplicates in this workshop RNA-seq workflow. Multiple reads at the same position can represent high gene expression rather than PCR duplication, so removing them can bias counts.


3.5.5 Index and summarize the filtered BAM
The filtered BAM is also indexed and summarized with samtools flagstat. Comparing the summaries before and after filtering shows how many alignments were removed. Finally, the temporary SAM is deleted because the sorted BAM contains the alignment information in a smaller, more useful form.


3.5.6 Run the mapping workflow
docker run --rm \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/work" \
  -w /work \
  docker.io/fgualdr/ngs-bowtie2-samtools \
  bash scripts/day2_rnaseq/02_map_bowtie2_sort_index.sh
Check the mapping logs:
ls -lh results/logs/day2/*.bowtie2.log
cat results/logs/day2/*.bowtie2.log
Bowtie2 logs report useful mapping metrics, including:







Metric
What it tells us




Number of input read pairs
Whether the aligner saw the expected amount of data


Concordantly aligned pairs
Read pairs that align with expected orientation and distance


Discordantly aligned pairs
Pairs that align but not in the expected paired-end pattern


Unaligned reads or pairs
Reads that did not match the reference well enough


Multiple alignment rate
Reads compatible with more than one genomic location


Overall alignment rate
Main first-pass check for whether the sample, reference, and FASTQ files make sense



Low mapping percentage can indicate a wrong reference, contamination, poor read quality, wrong sample labels, incomplete trimming, or strong rRNA/technical content.


3.5.7 Inspect the BAM summaries and outputs
Check the samtools flagstat summaries before and after filtering:
ls -lh results/logs/day2/*.flagstat.txt
cat results/logs/day2/*.flagstat.txt
These files help answer:

how many reads were mapped;
how many read pairs were properly paired;
how many alignments were removed by filtering;
whether one sample behaves very differently from the others.

Expected BAM outputs:
results/day2_rnaseq/bam/*.sorted.bam
results/day2_rnaseq/bam/*.sorted.bam.bai
results/day2_rnaseq/bam/*.filtered.bam
results/day2_rnaseq/bam/*.filtered.bam.bai
The *.sorted.bam files preserve all alignments for diagnosis. The *.filtered.bam files are the inputs to featureCounts.



3.6 Determine RNA-seq library strandedness
Genes are transcribed from either the + or the - genomic strand. RNA-seq library preparation determines whether the orientation of read 1 (R1) retains information about the strand of the original transcript. featureCounts needs this information so that a fragment is assigned only to a gene with the expected orientation.








Relationship between R1 and the transcript
Library type
featureCounts setting




R1 orientation is unrelated to transcript orientation
Unstranded
-s 0 (the default)


R1 has the same orientation as the transcript
Forward/sense stranded
-s 1


R1 has the opposite orientation to the transcript
Reverse/antisense stranded
-s 2



The published methods describe E-MTAB-13025 as an rRNA-depleted directional prokaryotic paired-end library using strand-selective second-strand chemistry and USER treatment. This library-preparation strategy is expected to produce a reverse-stranded library, in which R1 is opposite to the annotated transcript. This corresponds to featureCounts -s 2.
We nevertheless validate the orientation empirically on the actual workshop BAM files before counting. The RSeQC result agrees with the library-preparation information and supports -s 2.
Use infer_experiment.py from RSeQC together with the 12-column BED gene model created by the Day 1 reference script:
reference_genome/genes.bed
This BED file must describe the same GCF_025998455.1 assembly as the BAM files and must use the same sequence name, NZ_AP026446.1. A BED file made for the study’s original NC_000915.1 alignment cannot be used with the workshop BAM files.
During the workshop we inspected one BAM. The code below loops through every filtered BAM and saves the complete RSeQC report to one log file. infer_experiment.py writes the report to standard output, so we combine standard output and standard error and pass both through tee.
mkdir -p results/logs/day2

{
for f in results/day2_rnaseq/bam/*.filtered.bam; do
    echo
    echo "===== $f ====="

    docker run --rm \
      --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
      -v "$PWD:/work" \
      -w /work \
      docker.io/getwilds/rseqc \
      infer_experiment.py \
      -i "$f" \
      -r reference_genome/genes.bed

done
} 2>&1 | tee results/logs/day2/rseqc_strandedness.log
For paired-end data, the RSeQC strings encode the read number, the strand on which that read aligns, and the annotated transcript strand. For example, 1++ means that R1 aligns to the + genomic strand over a + transcript.








Dominant RSeQC result
Meaning
Use with featureCounts




The two orientation classes are approximately equal, often near 50/50
R1 orientation is unrelated to transcript orientation
-s 0

R1 has the same orientation as the transcript
-s 1

R1 has the opposite orientation to the transcript

title: Day 2 - RNA-seq from FASTQ to differential expression
section: 4. Count reads per gene with featureCounts
text:
4. Count reads per gene with featureCounts
The library preparation and the empirical RSeQC check both support reverse strandedness, so we use -s 2 for this dataset. We can now use featureCounts to obtain one raw fragment count per gene and sample:
filtered BAM + reference_genome/annotation.gff3
  -> featureCounts
  -> one complete featureCounts table
  -> select the gene and sample-count columns later in R
We keep the complete featureCounts table unchanged. In the R section, we will explicitly retain its gene identifier and sample-count columns and leave out the extra annotation columns that DESeq2 does not need.
Create scripts/day2_rnaseq/03_featurecounts_all_samples.sh:
nano scripts/day2_rnaseq/03_featurecounts_all_samples.sh
Paste this script:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

annotation="reference_genome/annotation.gff3"
bam_dir="results/day2_rnaseq/bam"
counts_dir="results/day2_rnaseq/counts"
log_dir="results/logs/day2"
featurecounts_out="${counts_dir}/featureCounts_all_samples.txt"

mkdir -p "${counts_dir}" "${log_dir}"

if [[ ! -f "${annotation}" ]]; then
  echo "ERROR: annotation file not found: ${annotation}" >&2
  exit 1
fi

bam_files=("${bam_dir}"/*.filtered.bam)

if [[ ! -e "${bam_files[0]}" ]]; then
  echo "ERROR: No filtered BAM files found in ${bam_dir}" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Counting reads across ${#bam_files[@]} samples"

featureCounts \
  -T 2 \
  -p \
  --countReadPairs \
  -B \
  -C \
  -s 2 \
  -t gene \
  -g ID \
  -a "${annotation}" \
  -o "${featurecounts_out}" \
  "${bam_files[@]}" \
  2>&1 | tee "${log_dir}/featureCounts_all_samples.log"

echo "Wrote ${featurecounts_out}"
The script performs these steps:







Code
Meaning




annotation=...
Store the path to the GFF3 annotation used to define genes.


bam_dir=..., counts_dir=..., log_dir=...
Store the input and output folder paths.


mkdir -p
Create the count and log folders if they do not exist.


bam_files=(.../*.filtered.bam)
Collect every filtered RNA-seq BAM file into a Bash array.


featureCounts
Count alignments that overlap annotated genes.


-T 2
Use two processing threads.


-p
Tell featureCounts that the BAM files contain paired-end reads.


--countReadPairs
Count one fragment for each read pair instead of counting the two read ends separately.


-B
Count a fragment only when both ends are aligned.


-C
Exclude chimeric pairs whose two ends align to different chromosomes.


-s 2
Count the library as reverse stranded: R1 is expected to align opposite to the annotated transcript strand, as supported by the library preparation and RSeQC.


-t gene
Count overlaps with GFF3 records whose feature type is gene.


-g ID
Use the GFF3 ID attribute as the gene identifier. This keeps the count identifiers consistent with the Day 1 BED12 gene model and the Day 4 annotation-based integration.


-a "${annotation}"
Supply the annotation file.


-o "${featurecounts_out}"
Write the complete count table to this file.


"${bam_files[@]}"
Pass all filtered BAM files to one featureCounts command, producing one count column per sample.


2>&1 \| tee ...
Show the featureCounts messages in the terminal and save the same messages in a log file.



The chosen -s value is also study-specific and must follow the metadata or empirical RSeQC result.

  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/work" \

Check the featureCounts logs:

head results/day2_rnaseq/counts/featureCounts_all_samples.txt
cat results/day2_rnaseq/counts/featureCounts_all_samples.txt.summary
These logs tell us how many aligned fragments were assigned to genes. This is a second sanity check after mapping. A sample can map well but count poorly if the annotation does not match the genome, the wrong feature type is used, the library strandedness is wrong, or many reads fall outside annotated genes.
The complete featureCounts table should look like this:
Geneid  Chr           Start  End  Strand  Length  results/day2_rnaseq/bam/WT_1.filtered.bam  ...
geneA   NZ_AP026446.1  100    450  +       351     120                                                   ...
geneB   NZ_AP026446.1  600    900  -       301     5                                                     ...
The first six columns describe each annotated gene. Every later column contains the raw fragment counts for one BAM file. Do not edit this table manually or convert its counts to CPM, TPM, RPKM, or bigWig signal before DESeq2. We will select and rename the required columns in R.
Approximate sanity checks before moving to DESeq2:








Check
Reasonable workshop expectation
If it looks bad




Bowtie2 overall alignment rate
Often high for a small bacterial genome when the reference and sample labels are correct
Check wrong reference, contamination, mixed samples, or failed trimming


Properly paired reads after filtering
Most mapped pairs should remain properly paired
Check R1/R2 pairing, sample names, insert size, or over-strict filtering


featureCounts assignment rate
A large fraction of aligned fragments should assign to annotated genes in a compact bacterial genome
Check annotation/reference mismatch, -t/-g options, strandedness, or chromosome names


Replicate behavior
Replicates should have broadly similar mapping, assignment, and library sizes
Recheck sample labels and any sample-specific QC warning



These are qualitative checks, not pass/fail statistical tests. A clearly different sample should be investigated before interpreting differential expression.

title: Day 2 - RNA-seq from FASTQ to differential expression
section: 5. From a count matrix to differential expression with DESeq2
text:
5. From a count matrix to differential expression with DESeq2
The featureCounts table gives us one integer count per gene and sample. At this point the main question changes:

Are the differences we observe between conditions larger than we would expect from biological and sampling variability?

Before answering that question, we first need to understand what DESeq2 is, why it is commonly used, what assumptions it makes, and how the experimental design enters the analysis.

5.1 Why DESeq2?
There is no single differential-expression tool for RNA-seq. Widely used alternatives include edgeR, limma-voom, DSS, and others. In this workshop we use DESeq2 because it has become one of the de facto reference frameworks for bulk RNA-seq differential expression: it is widely used, well documented, supports simple and complex experimental designs, and links normalization, dispersion estimation, generalized linear models, statistical testing, diagnostics, and result extraction in one coherent workflow.
DESeq2 is an R/Bioconductor package. In everyday speech, R packages are often called libraries, although technically a package is the bundled collection of functions, classes, documentation, and supporting data, while library(DESeq2) loads that package into the current R session. DESeq2 is therefore not one single test: it is a set of interlinked functions operating on the same DESeqDataSet object and together implementing a complete statistical workflow.
The main DESeq2 reference is:

Love MI, Huber W, Anders S. Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2. Genome Biology 15, 550 (2014). doi:10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8


A little historical context
RNA-seq counts are not well described by a simple Gaussian model, and biological replicates usually vary more than expected from a Poisson process. This became particularly important in early RNA-seq experiments, where only a few biological replicates per condition were common.
A major step was therefore to model RNA-seq as overdispersed count data and to borrow information across thousands of genes instead of estimating the variance of every gene completely independently.








Period / framework
Main idea
Why it mattered




Early simple approaches
Poisson models, transformed expression values, or tests not designed specifically for overdispersed sequencing counts
Often underestimated biological variability or handled the mean-variance relationship poorly


edgeR / DESeq (DESeq1)
Negative-binomial models and sharing information across genes to estimate variability with few replicates
Made biological replication and overdispersion central to RNA-seq inference


DESeq2
Negative-binomial GLMs, moderated gene-wise dispersion estimates, model-based coefficient SEs, Wald/LRT inference, flexible design formulas, independent filtering and outlier diagnostics
Generalized the approach into a more flexible regression framework suitable for both simple and multi-factor experiments



The original DESeq method already modeled counts with a negative-binomial distribution and estimated the relationship between mean expression and variability across genes using a smooth trend Anders & Huber, 2010. DESeq2 retained the same broad principle but moved the analysis into a unified negative-binomial generalized linear model (GLM) framework and introduced improved shrinkage/moderation of dispersion and, historically, fold-change estimates. Current DESeq2 separates log2-fold-change shrinkage into lfcShrink() rather than applying it automatically during the main Wald test.






Note



Take-home: DESeq2 did not invent RNA-seq differential expression, and it is not the only valid method. We use it because it is a mature, widely adopted implementation of the general principle: model count data, estimate biological variability using information shared across genes, fit the experimental design, and test the effect of interest.





5.2 The DESeq2 idea without the mathematics
DESeq2 starts from raw integer counts. The counts must remain on a count scale because the model is built for discrete sequencing counts. Do not convert the input matrix to CPM, TPM, RPKM, percentages, log values, or bigWig signal before fitting DESeq2.
Individual libraries are sequenced to different depths. A count of 500 in one sample therefore does not necessarily represent the same abundance as a count of 500 in another sample. DESeq2 first estimates a sample-specific size factor so that differences in overall library size are accounted for internally.
For each gene, the conceptual workflow is:
RAW INTEGER COUNTS
        |
        v
account for differences in library size
        |
        v
fit a GLM describing the EXPECTED COUNT
for each sample from the experimental design
        |
        v
ask how much the OBSERVED COUNTS vary
around those fitted expectations
        |
        v
model that variability with a gene-specific
NEGATIVE-BINOMIAL DISPERSION alpha_i
        |
        v
stabilize alpha_i by borrowing information
from the genome-wide mean-dispersion trend
        |
        v
use the stabilized dispersion + fitted means
+ design + number of biological replicates
        |
        v
estimate the uncertainty of the condition effect:
SE(log2FC)
        |
        v
z = log2FC / SE(log2FC)
        |
        v
Wald-test p-value
        |
        v
multiple-testing correction
        |
        v
adjusted p-value / FDR
Three quantities should remain conceptually distinct:







Quantity
Interpretation




Expected count
Count predicted by the fitted model for a gene in a sample after accounting for library size and the design


Dispersion alpha_i
How variable the observed counts for gene i are around their fitted expectations


SE(log2FC)
How uncertain we are about the estimated condition effect



With only a few biological replicates, a completely independent dispersion estimate for every gene would be unstable. DESeq2 therefore learns the typical relationship between mean expression and dispersion across all genes and moderates each gene-specific dispersion toward that trend. By default DESeq2 tries a parametric mean-dispersion trend; if that shape is unsuitable, a local fit can be used instead.
The stabilized dispersion is not itself the standard error of the fold change. It is one of the quantities used by the fitted GLM to determine the uncertainty of the estimated coefficient.


5.3 The experimental design: decide what the model should explain
The design formula is not a software detail. It is the statistical representation of the experimental structure.
A good rule is:

Include variables that represent real, identifiable sources of systematic variation that should be accounted for while estimating the biological effect of interest. Do not add columns simply because they exist in the metadata.

The experimental unit matters more than the column name. In particular, a metadata column called replicate does not automatically belong in the model.








Experimental structure
Typical DESeq2 design
Principle




Two independent conditions with biological replicates
~ condition
Replicate numbers are identifiers, not covariates


Same patient / donor / animal measured in both conditions
~ subject + condition
Subject is a blocking factor because measurements are paired


Samples processed in different technical batches, with conditions represented across batches
~ batch + condition
Account for systematic batch variation while estimating condition


Genotype and treatment where treatment effect may differ by genotype
~ genotype + treatment + genotype:treatment
Use an interaction only when the scientific question is about different responses


Same biological library sequenced twice
Collapse technical runs before DESeq2
Multiple sequencing runs of the same library are not independent biological replicates


Batch and condition perfectly confounded
No valid formula can separate them
The experiment itself does not contain enough information to estimate both effects




Biological replicate versus blocking factor
For this workshop we have three control and three treated samples. The metadata labels them as replicate 1, 2, and 3 within each condition, but those replicate numbers are simply identifiers for independent biological replicates. Replicate 1 in control is not a repeated measurement of the same biological unit as replicate 1 in treated.
Therefore our workshop model is:
design = ~ conditions
and not:
design = ~ replicates + conditions
Adding an arbitrary replicate-number factor would incorrectly tell the model that samples carrying the same number form matched blocks.
By contrast, if the experiment contained samples from the same patient before and after treatment, the patient identity would represent genuine pairing and we would use:
design = ~ patient + condition


General principles when choosing covariates

Define the biological question and experimental unit first, then write the design.
Include known batch or subject effects when they are biologically/statistically meaningful and not perfectly confounded with the condition of interest.
Do not treat technical replicates as independent biological evidence.
Do not include an arbitrary replicate number simply to “account for replicates”; biological replication is what allows dispersion to be estimated in the first place.
Avoid adding many covariates to a very small experiment unless they are essential: every additional coefficient consumes information.
Prefer variables specified from the experimental design or strong prior knowledge, not variables selected because they make the desired p-values smaller.
If a covariate is perfectly confounded with condition, no statistical model can recover the two effects separately; this is a design problem rather than a DESeq2 problem.
For convenience and interpretability, put the main variable of interest last in the formula and set its reference level explicitly.







Warning



Model design is part of the experiment. A sophisticated model cannot recover information that was never separated experimentally. If all controls were processed in batch 1 and all treated samples in batch 2, batch and condition are indistinguishable.





5.4 Why PCA before differential expression?
Before testing genes one by one, we should first ask whether the samples themselves behave as expected.
NGS experiments typically contain thousands of measured features but relatively few samples. We therefore need sample-level exploratory analyses that summarize the global structure of the data without starting from a list of significant genes.
Principal component analysis (PCA) is widely used for this purpose because it is unsupervised: the PCA calculation does not know which samples are controls, treated, batch 1, batch 2, or potential outliers. It simply finds the major directions of variation across the expression profiles. We add biological labels only afterwards to interpret the pattern.
In RNA-seq QC, PCA helps us ask:

Do biological replicates occupy similar regions of expression space?
Is the largest source of variation related to the biological condition we intended to study?
Is there an unexpected batch structure?
Does one sample behave very differently from all others?
Could a sample label have been swapped?
Is a putative outlier also unusual in mapping rate, library size, gene assignment, or other QC metrics?

For PCA, each sample is treated as one point described by the expression of many genes. PCA replaces those thousands of gene dimensions with a smaller set of principal components. PC1 captures the largest direction of sample-to-sample variation, PC2 the largest remaining independent direction, and so on. A PC1-versus-PC2 plot is therefore a low-dimensional view of the strongest global structure in the experiment.






Important



PCA is a diagnostic, not an automatic outlier-removal algorithm.
A sample should not be removed simply because it lies far from the other points or because removing it improves the differential-expression result. A PCA outlier should trigger investigation of sample identity, FASTQ/BAM QC, mapping, strandedness, gene assignment, library size, batch metadata, and laboratory notes. Exclusion is defensible when there is evidence of technical failure, contamination, mislabelling, or another pre-specified reason. If the sample reflects genuine biological heterogeneity, removing it can bias the analysis.


In this workshop we use log2(normalized_counts + 1) for PCA because it keeps the transformation transparent. In larger RNA-seq analyses, DESeq2 vst() or rlog() are commonly used to reduce the strong dependence of variance on mean expression before PCA and clustering.


5.5 Wald test, multiple testing and FDR
After the model has estimated the condition effect and its standard error for each gene, the Wald statistic is simply the effect expressed in units of its uncertainty:
z = log2FC / SE(log2FC)
A large absolute z means that the estimated effect is large relative to the uncertainty of that estimate. Under the null hypothesis of no condition effect, DESeq2 compares this statistic with the standard normal distribution to obtain a p-value.
RNA-seq tests hundreds or thousands of genes simultaneously. Even if no true biological effects existed, some small p-values would occur by chance. DESeq2 therefore reports a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value (padj), which is used to control the false discovery rate (FDR).
At an FDR threshold of 5%, the procedure aims to keep the expected fraction of false discoveries among the genes called significant at about 5% or below. This is not the same as saying that each individual gene with padj < 0.05 has a 5% probability of being a false positive.


5.6 Build and inspect the DESeq2 analysis interactively
We will build the R analysis during the workshop instead of immediately running a finished script. Each block will be:

typed into scripts/day2_rnaseq/04_deseq2_analysis.R in VS Code;
copied into an interactive R session;
inspected before we continue.

The saved script remains the reproducible record of the analysis, while the interactive session lets us see what each object contains.
From the root of workshop_ngs, launch R inside the Bioconductor image:
docker run --rm -it \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/work" \
  -w /work \
  docker.io/fgualdr/ngs-r-bioc \
  R --vanilla
The -it options keep the terminal attached to R. The project is mounted at /work, so scripts and results written there remain on the laptop after the container closes.
When the R prompt (>) appears, confirm the working directory:
getwd()
list.files()
getwd() should return "/work".
Keep this R session open. In the VS Code Explorer, create scripts/day2_rnaseq/04_deseq2_analysis.R. Type each block below into that file, save it, and then copy the same lines into the R prompt. Do not copy the > prompt itself.
Use one continuous script for the analysis. We will run and comment the same code interactively, but keeping it in one file makes the complete sequence of operations easy to follow and reproducible.






NoteCheckpoint: raw RNA-seq count table



If mapping or feature counting could not be completed on your laptop, you can continue the workshop from the instructor-provided raw featureCounts table.
Download featureCounts_all_samples.txt Download count_matrix_hpylori.txt
Save the downloaded file as:
results/day2_rnaseq/counts/featureCounts_all_samples.txt
Alternatively we can start from the original data of the Paper whihc includes all the conditions.
results/day2_rnaseq/counts/count_matrix_hpylori.txt


#!/usr/bin/env Rscript

library(DESeq2)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

count_file <- "results/day2_rnaseq/counts/featureCounts_all_samples.txt"
out_dir <- "results/day2_rnaseq/deseq2"
count_matrix_file <- "results/day2_rnaseq/counts/gene_count_matrix.tsv"

dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Import featureCounts output and prepare the raw count matrix
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

featureCounts <- read.delim(count_file, sep = "\t", comment.char = "#", check.names = FALSE)

colnames(featureCounts) <- gsub("results/day2_rnaseq/bam/", "", colnames(featureCounts), fixed = TRUE)
colnames(featureCounts) <- gsub(".filtered.bam", "", colnames(featureCounts), fixed = TRUE)
rownames(featureCounts) <- featureCounts$Geneid

# Keep only sample-count columns
featureCounts <- featureCounts[,grep("^WT",colnames(featureCounts))]
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Build the sample design
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

design_dt <- data.frame(
    samples = colnames(featureCounts),
    conditions = gsub("_1|_2|_3","",colnames(featureCounts)),
    replicates = gsub("WT_","",gsub("WTS_","",colnames(featureCounts)))
)

design_dt$conditions[design_dt$conditions == "WT"] <- "control"
design_dt$conditions[design_dt$conditions == "WTS"] <- "treated"
design_dt$conditions <- factor(design_dt$conditions, levels = c("control", "treated"))

rownames(design_dt) <- design_dt$samples

# Put the design rows in exactly the same order as the count columns
design_dt <- design_dt[colnames(featureCounts), , drop = FALSE]
featureCounts <- featureCounts[, rownames(design_dt), drop = FALSE]

# Save the clean raw count matrix
count_out <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(featureCounts), featureCounts, check.names = FALSE)
write.table(count_out, count_matrix_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Create the DESeq2 dataset
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

dds <- DESeq2::DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = as.matrix(featureCounts),
  colData = design_dt,
  design = ~ conditions
)

# inspect the content using attributes(dds)!

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Estimate library-size factors BEFORE fitting the full model
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

dds <- DESeq2::estimateSizeFactors(dds)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PCA on log2-normalized counts: inspect sample relationships and outliers
# Before diving into DEGs we check if the expected biological perturbation is the main driver of the variation in the experiment!
# Use PCA
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
normalized_counts <- DESeq2::counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)
pca_input <- log2(normalized_counts+1) 
# Here there are different ways to treat the count data before PCA!
# log, scale, center, center+scale, Yeo-Johnson, Box-Cox, Quantile, etc...

pca <- prcomp(
  t(pca_input),
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = FALSE
)

variance_explained <- 100 * (pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2))

pca_dt <- data.frame(
  sample = rownames(pca$x),
  PC1 = pca$x[, 1],
  PC2 = pca$x[, 2],
  conditions = design_dt[rownames(pca$x), "conditions"],
  replicates = design_dt[rownames(pca$x), "replicates"]
)

pca_plot <- ggplot(pca_dt, aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = conditions, shape = replicates, label = sample)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", variance_explained[1]),
    y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", variance_explained[2])
  )

ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "pc1_pc2_pca.pdf"), pca_plot, width = 6, height = 5)

scree_dt <- data.frame(
  PC = seq_along(variance_explained),
  variance = variance_explained
)

scree_plot <- ggplot(scree_dt, aes(x=PC, y=variance)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scree_dt$PC) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Principal component", y = "Variance explained (%)")

ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "pca_scree.pdf"), scree_plot, width = 6, height = 4)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fit the DESeq2 model and extract treated versus control
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

dds <- DESeq2::DESeq(dds, fitType = "parametric")

print(DESeq2::resultsNames(dds))

res2 <- DESeq2::results(
  dds,
  contrast = c("conditions", "treated", "control") # treated vs control so control is the denominator!
)

res_dt <- as.data.frame(res2)
res_dt$gene_id <- rownames(res_dt)

write.table(
  res_dt, 
  file.path(out_dir, "deseq2_results.tsv"),
  sep = "\t", 
  quote = FALSE, 
  row.names = FALSE
  )

ranked <- res_dt[!is.na(res_dt$padj), , drop = FALSE]

ranked <- ranked[order(ranked$padj, abs(ranked$log2FoldChange)), , drop = FALSE]

normalized_counts <- DESeq2::counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)

l <- list()
for(cond in unique(design_dt$conditions)){
  idx <- which(
    colnames(normalized_counts)  %in% rownames(design_dt[design_dt$conditions == cond,])
    )
  a <- normalized_counts[, idx]
  a <- rowMeans(a)
  l[[cond]] <- a
}
av_l <- as.data.frame(do.call(cbind,l))
av_l <- av_l[,c("control","treated")]

ranked <- cbind(ranked,av_l[rownames(ranked),])

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dispersion plot
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

pdf(file.path(out_dir, "dispersion_plot.pdf"))
  DESeq2::plotDispEsts(dds)
dev.off()

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Custom MA-like plot: mean expression versus log2 fold change
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Use a signed significance score:
# significant down-regulated genes -> negative -> blue
# non-significant genes            -> 0        -> white
# significant up-regulated genes   -> positive -> red
res_dt$signed_significance <- 0
is_sig <- !is.na(res_dt$padj) & res_dt$padj < 0.05
res_dt$signed_significance[is_sig] <-
  sign(res_dt$log2FoldChange[is_sig]) * -log10(pmax(res_dt$padj[is_sig], .Machine$double.xmin))

sig_dt <- res_dt[is_sig, , drop = FALSE]

top_up <- sig_dt[sig_dt$log2FoldChange > 0, , drop = FALSE]
top_up <- head(top_up[order(top_up$padj, -top_up$log2FoldChange), , drop = FALSE], 5)

top_down <- sig_dt[sig_dt$log2FoldChange < 0, , drop = FALSE]
top_down <- head(top_down[order(top_down$padj, top_down$log2FoldChange), , drop = FALSE], 5)

label_dt <- rbind(top_up, top_down)

ma_plot <- ggplot(res_dt, aes(baseMean + 1, log2FoldChange, color = signed_significance)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.9, size = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0,
    name = "signed\n-log10(padj)"
  ) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = label_dt,
    aes(label = gene_id),
    size = 3,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Mean normalized expression (baseMean + 1, log10 scale)",
    y = "log2 fold change (treated / control)"
  )

ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "ma_plot.pdf"), ma_plot, width = 7, height = 5)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Volcano plot
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

res_dt$minus_log10_padj <- -log10(pmax(res_dt$padj, .Machine$double.xmin))

volcano <- ggplot(res_dt, aes(log2FoldChange, minus_log10_padj)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "log2 fold change (treated / control)",
    y = "-log10 adjusted p-value"
  )

ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "volcano.pdf"), volcano, width = 6, height = 5)

writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path(out_dir, "sessionInfo.txt"))

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We will save usefull data for the generation of scaled Tracks!
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

size_factors <- DESeq2::sizeFactors(dds)
normalized_counts <- DESeq2::counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)
normalized_out <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(normalized_counts), normalized_counts, check.names = FALSE)

write.table(
  normalized_out, 
  file.path(out_dir, "normalized_counts.tsv"),
  sep = "\t", 
  quote = FALSE, 
  row.names = FALSE
  )

# DESeq2 divides counts by the size factor.
# Later we will use bamCoverage to create BigWig tracks
# bamCoverage  multiplies coverage by --scaleFactor.
# Therefore the matching bamCoverage factor is 1 / DESeq2 size factor.
scale_dt <- data.frame(
  sample = names(size_factors),
  deseq2_size_factor = as.numeric(size_factors),
  bamcoverage_scale_factor = 1 / as.numeric(size_factors) 
  # this as Deseq2 divide so scales down to the lower. BamCoverage used for BigWig generation instead uses multiplicative scaling
)

write.table(scale_dt, file.path(out_dir, "deseq2_size_factors.tsv"),
            sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)

print(scale_dt)



5.7 Read the analysis in the same order DESeq2 performs it
The code above contains many R commands, but conceptually the workflow is short.

Step 1: raw count matrix + metadata
The rows are genes and the columns are samples. The counts remain integer fragment counts from featureCounts. The metadata describes which samples are control or treated.
The order must match exactly:
count-matrix columns  ==  metadata rows
DESeq2 does not infer sample identity from filenames once the matrix has been constructed.


Step 2: size factors
Libraries differ in sequencing depth and overall count scale. DESeq2 estimates one size factor per sample so that counts from different libraries can be compared on a common scale.
We save normalized counts for exploration and visualization, but the statistical model still uses the original raw counts together with the size factors.


Step 3: PCA as sample-level QC
We run PCA before interpreting differential expression. The important questions are not whether the conditions separate perfectly, but whether the global sample structure makes biological and technical sense.
For this six-sample experiment:
6 samples x many genes
        |
        v
log2-normalized expression
        |
        v
PCA
        |
        v
PC1 / PC2 sample map
Each point is one sample. Samples close together have broadly similar global expression profiles; samples far apart differ across many genes. Because PCA is unsupervised, unexpected separation can reveal batch effects or sample problems that would otherwise be hidden by looking only at the final DEG table.


Step 4: fit the DESeq2 model
For this experiment we use:
design = ~ conditions
The coefficient of interest compares:
treated / control
Therefore:
positive log2FoldChange  -> higher expression in treated samples
negative log2FoldChange  -> lower expression in treated samples
When DESeq() runs, it carries out the major stages discussed above: size-factor estimation, gene-wise dispersion estimation, fitting/stabilizing the genome-wide dispersion trend, negative-binomial GLM fitting, and coefficient testing.


Step 5: inspect the dispersion plot
The dispersion plot shows how gene-level variability changes with mean expression and how noisy gene-wise dispersion estimates are stabilized using information from the full set of genes.
The point is not to memorize the exact curve. The important idea is:

genes with similar expression provide information about the amount of variability we should expect when replication is limited.



Step 6: interpret the results table
The main DESeq2 columns are:



Column
Meaning




baseMean
Mean normalized expression across samples


log2FoldChange
Estimated treated-versus-control effect


lfcSE
Standard error of that estimated log2 fold change


stat
Wald statistic: effect divided by its SE


pvalue
Unadjusted p-value for this gene


padj
Multiple-testing-adjusted p-value used for FDR control



The effect size and statistical evidence are related but not interchangeable. A large fold change can be uncertain when counts are low or variable, while a modest fold change can be estimated precisely when counts are high and replicates are consistent.


Step 7: use plots to answer different questions
PCA asks whether the samples show sensible global structure before gene-level interpretation.
Dispersion plot asks whether the estimated gene variability follows a coherent mean-dispersion relationship and shows the moderation performed by DESeq2.
MA-like plot shows effect size against mean expression:
x-axis = mean normalized expression
 y-axis = log2 fold change
It is useful for seeing whether large fold changes are concentrated among low-count genes and for inspecting the dependence of effect estimates on abundance.
Volcano plot combines effect size and statistical evidence:
x-axis = log2 fold change
 y-axis = -log10 adjusted p-value
A volcano plot is a presentation of the fitted results, not the statistical model itself. Always interpret it together with the count structure, PCA, dispersion, and MA plot.
When the interactive inspection is finished, leave R with:
q(save = "no")
The container is removed, but the script and all files written under /work remain on the laptop.

title: Day 2 - RNA-seq from FASTQ to differential expression
section: 6. Optional: make RNA-seq bigWig tracks with the DESeq2 size factors
text:
6. Optional: make RNA-seq bigWig tracks with the DESeq2 size factors
bigWig files store genome-wide coverage signal. They are useful for IGV inspection but are not inputs to DESeq2.
Here we deliberately reuse the library-size normalization estimated by DESeq2. DESeq2 normalizes by dividing counts by each sample’s size factor. bamCoverage --scaleFactor, instead, multiplies the coverage values by the supplied factor. We therefore saved the inverse factor (1 / size factor) in deseq2_size_factors.tsv.
Create scripts/day2_rnaseq/05_make_bigwig_bamcoverage.sh:
nano scripts/day2_rnaseq/05_make_bigwig_bamcoverage.sh
Paste this script:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

bam_dir="results/day2_rnaseq/bam"
out_dir="results/day2_rnaseq/bigwig"
log_dir="results/logs/day2"
scale_file="results/day2_rnaseq/deseq2/deseq2_size_factors.tsv"

mkdir -p "${out_dir}" "${log_dir}"


while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample deseq2_size_factor bamcoverage_scale_factor
do
  bam="${bam_dir}/${sample}.filtered.bam"

  echo "${sample}: DESeq2 size factor=${deseq2_size_factor}; bamCoverage scale factor=${bamcoverage_scale_factor}"

  bamCoverage \
    -b "${bam}" \
    -o "${out_dir}/${sample}.deseq2.bw" \
    --scaleFactor "${bamcoverage_scale_factor}" \
    --binSize 10 \
    --numberOfProcessors 2 \
    2>&1 | tee "${log_dir}/${sample}.bamCoverage.log"
done < <(tail -n +2 "${scale_file}")
Run it:
docker run --rm \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/work" \
  -w /work \
  docker.io/fgualdr/ngs-deeptools \
  bash scripts/day2_rnaseq/05_make_bigwig_bamcoverage.sh
Expected output:
results/day2_rnaseq/bigwig/*.deseq2.bw
Each sample produces one total-coverage bigWig named *.deseq2.bw. These tracks use the same sample-specific multiplicative scaling implied by the DESeq2 size factors. They are intended for visualization and sample comparison; DESeq2 itself still uses the raw integer gene counts as input.

NoteDocker users and files written into the workshop folder… something I did not know!



When a container writes into a folder mounted from your laptop, the files are created using the numeric user and group IDs of the process running inside the container. Workshop commands that mount the project therefore use:
--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"
id -u and id -g return the numeric UID and GID of your current macOS, Linux, or Ubuntu/WSL2 user. Passing them to Docker makes files written into the mounted project belong to the same user instead of to root or to a different user defined inside the image.
The problem is not always obvious on every computer. On native Linux and Ubuntu/WSL2, bind-mounted files follow Linux ownership rules directly: a container running as root may write successfully but leave root-owned files, whereas a container running as another non-root UID may receive Permission denied. On macOS, Docker Desktop runs Linux containers inside a VM and mediates access to the macOS filesystem, so UID/GID differences are often translated or less visible.
This is especially worth remembering for images built from Conda/Mamba/Micromamba base images. Such images may deliberately run as a dedicated non-root user (for example mambauser) whose UID/GID is unrelated to the user on the laptop. --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" explicitly overrides that runtime identity for workshop commands that write into the mounted project.

title: Day 0 - Technical setup for a reproducible NGS workshop
Reproducible NGS Data Analysis
text:
Welcome
Modern sequencing projects require much more than running bioinformatics tools.
Throughout the workshop, reproducible analysis = inputs/provenance + code/parameters + software environment. The exact reference assembly belongs to the first component, and digest-pinned container images identify the third.
A reproducible analysis requires:
metadata retrieval
-> raw data retrieval
-> workflow execution
-> design-specific analysis
-> documentation
-> version control
This workshop introduces a practical workflow for organizing, executing, documenting, and interpreting RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses using public datasets and lightweight computational infrastructure.
The practical examples focus on bacterial genomes and small datasets that can be explored on personal laptops, while introducing concepts that can also scale to larger projects and institutional computing environments.






Important



This workshop teaches a reproducible approach to RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analysis using public sequencing datasets, containers, Git/GitHub, and structured project documentation.
Rather than focusing on a single software package, the workshop emphasizes workflows that can be understood, reproduced, shared, and adapted to real research projects.
The goal is to give you practical experience with the core steps of reference-based NGS analysis and to provide a project framework that you can reuse in your own research or laboratory work.





Learning objectives
By the end of the workshop, you should be able to:

Create a reproducible NGS project structure
Use Git and GitHub to document analyses
Use Docker containers to run bioinformatics tools
Retrieve public sequencing datasets through the GEO/SRA and ArrayExpress collection in BioStudies/ENA routes
Generate and interpret quality-control reports
Perform basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses
Produce differential expression and peak-calling results
Associate regulatory regions with nearby genes
Document and communicate results through reports and figures




Workshop structure







Day
Main topic




Day 0
Setup and readiness


Day 1
Reproducible project setup, FASTQ QC/trimming, and reference files


Day 2
RNA-seq workflow and analysis


Day 3
ChIP-seq workflow and analysis


Day 4
Data integration and reporting






What students will build
Students do not clone a finished analysis repository or copy a hidden template.
Instead, each participant progressively creates their own GitHub repository containing:

a clear project structure
metadata tables
analysis scripts
selected reports
figures
workflow documentation

By the end of the workshop, each student should have:

A reproducible GitHub repository
A documented RNA-seq and/or ChIP-seq workflow
A short report summarizing the analysis

The assembly of this repository will be used to evaluate student progress.



Datasets
The workshop uses publicly available datasets derived from small bacterial genomes.
The main examples are based on Helicobacter pylori strain N6 datasets generated to study the HP1021 redox switch regulon under microaerophilic and aerobic growth conditions:

Helicobacter pylori RNA-seq: E-MTAB-13025
Helicobacter pylori ChIP-seq: E-MTAB-13026

These datasets are associated with the publication:
Noszka M. et al. “Profiling of the Helicobacter pylori redox switch HP1021 regulon using a multi-omics approach.” Nature Communications (2023).

Publication: PubMed Central and Nature
RNA-seq dataset: E-MTAB-13025
ChIP-seq dataset: E-MTAB-13026

The full study includes multiple genotypes and analyses. In this workshop, we retain the wild-type samples: three biological replicates under microaerobic conditions and three under aerobic oxidative stress for each assay.
The publication provides biological context and raw-data provenance; it does not define the workshop reference coordinates. We reprocess the selected FASTQ files against the current NCBI RefSeq reference assembly GCF_025998455.1 (ASM2599845v1, strain CHC155; chromosome NZ_AP026446.1) using its matching RefSeq annotation. All BAM, bigWig, count, peak, and integration outputs are regenerated in that coordinate system rather than reused from the publication.
This is a simplified, laptop-scale reanalysis and is not expected to reproduce the paper’s coordinate-dependent results.

If this is your first visit, begin with:
Day 0 - Setup and readiness
Then continue through the lessons in sequence using the navigation panel on the left. Each day page will be released as the corresponding lesson becomes available.

Questions, problems, or suggestions should preferably be reported through the GitHub repository issue tracker. This makes the discussion visible, traceable, and useful for other participants who may encounter the same problem.
